name: The Raven Paradox
statement: Observing a green apple, which is a non-black non-raven, seems to confirm that all ravens are black.
statementAccent: seems to confirm that all ravens are black
meaning: The raven paradox, also called Hempel's ravens or the paradox of confirmation, is a puzzle about the logic of inductive support, proposed by the German logician and philosopher Carl Gustav Hempel in the 1940s. Consider the hypothesis that all ravens are black. It seems that observing a black raven confirms this hypothesis. But all ravens are black is logically equivalent to its contrapositive, all non-black things are non-ravens, and it seems that whatever confirms a statement also confirms anything logically equivalent to it. So observing a non-black non-raven, such as a green apple or a white shoe, confirms all non-black things are non-ravens and therefore also confirms that all ravens are black. The paradox is that one could apparently gather evidence about the colour of ravens by examining apples and shoes indoors, never looking at a raven at all, a conclusion Hempel wryly compared to indoor ornithology.
mechanism: The paradox is generated by three plausible principles that seem jointly to yield the absurd result. Nicod's criterion says a generalisation of the form all P are Q is confirmed by observing instances that are both P and Q, so a black raven confirms all ravens are black. The logical fact of contraposition says all ravens are black is equivalent to all non-black things are non-ravens. And the equivalence condition says that whatever confirms a hypothesis confirms any logically equivalent hypothesis. Putting these together, a non-black non-raven, being an instance of the contrapositive generalisation, confirms it and hence confirms the original. Since green apples and white shoes are non-black non-ravens, they confirm that all ravens are black, which seems absurd. The most influential resolution is Bayesian: observing a non-black non-raven really does confirm the hypothesis, but by an utterly negligible amount, because non-black non-ravens are vastly more numerous than ravens, so each such observation barely raises the probability. On this view the confirmation is genuine but so tiny that the sense of paradox dissolves. Hempel himself accepted the conclusion as only apparently paradoxical.

examples.text: All ravens are black is logically equivalent to all non-black things are non-ravens, so evidence for one is evidence for the other.
It seems one could confirm that all ravens are black by examining green apples and white shoes indoors, never observing a raven, which appears absurd.
A green apple does confirm the hypothesis, but by a negligible amount, since non-black non-ravens vastly outnumber ravens, so the effect is real but tiny.

variants.name: The Bayesian resolution
variants.text: The account, associated with I. J. Good, that non-black non-ravens confirm the hypothesis only negligibly because they are so much more numerous than ravens.

variants.name: Hempel's acceptance
variants.text: Hempel's own response of biting the bullet, holding the conclusion only seems paradoxical because background knowledge makes such observations feel irrelevant.

whyItMatters: The raven paradox is a central problem in confirmation theory and the philosophy of science, exposing tensions in the seemingly obvious idea that instances confirm generalisations. By deriving an absurd-looking conclusion from innocuous principles about evidence, logical equivalence, and confirmation, it forced philosophers to examine what it means for observations to support a hypothesis and drove the development of quantitative, Bayesian approaches to confirmation. The Bayesian resolution, that irrelevant-seeming evidence confirms only negligibly, became a model for how probability can rescue and refine intuitions about induction. The paradox remains a standard reference point in debates about inductive logic, the role of background knowledge, and the relation between logic and evidence, and its memorable image of confirming ornithology from an armchair keeps it a favourite teaching example.

working.text: start from all ravens are black and its contrapositive, all non-black things are non-ravens.
use Nicod's criterion and the equivalence condition to conclude that a non-black non-raven confirms both statements.
resolve the oddity by noting the confirmation from a green apple is genuine but negligible, since such objects vastly outnumber ravens.

limits: The raven paradox is a problem about the logic of confirmation rather than a claim that examining apples is a good way to study ravens; the Bayesian resolution grants that such evidence confirms only by a negligible amount, so in practice it is useless while in principle it is not zero. The resolution depends on assumptions about the relative numbers of ravens and non-black things and on a Bayesian framework that not everyone accepts, and alternative diagnoses reject one of the generating principles instead. Hempel's own bullet-biting response treats the conclusion as merely counterintuitive, shifting the burden to explaining the intuition rather than blocking the argument. So the paradox marks an ongoing issue in confirmation theory, with several proposed treatments, rather than a single settled fix.
misreadings: The paradox does not recommend confirming hypotheses about ravens by studying apples; the point is that such evidence, while technically confirming, is negligible, not useful. It is not resolved by denying that black ravens confirm the hypothesis, which they plainly do. And accepting the Bayesian dissolution does not mean the confirmation is exactly zero; it means it is vanishingly small, so treating the paradox as showing that logic is broken, or that induction is worthless, misreads a puzzle designed to refine how we understand evidence.
origin: Proposed by the philosopher Carl Gustav Hempel in the 1940s, in his work on the logic of confirmation, to show that plausible principles about evidence imply that a non-black non-raven confirms the hypothesis that all ravens are black.
